title: Hegemony and the Rise of Rival Powers
welcome_lead: Step into the geopolitical arena where the USA's hegemonic grip meets China's surging influence.
meta_desc: A-Level Geography Edexcel Superpowers: hegemony, BRICS rise, Mackinder, and Nye's power.
final_note: You have charted the shifting tectonics of 21st-century power.

concepts.def: Dominance of one state over others, politically and economically.
Nye's concept: influence via culture, values and diplomacy.
Influence via military force and economic coercion.
Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa emerging bloc.
Mackinder: control of Eurasia equals global control.
World order dominated by a single superpower.

walkthroughs.body_html: After the Soviet collapse in 1991, the USA emerged as the sole superpower, projecting hegemonic influence economically (Bretton Woods, IMF, World Bank), militarily (NATO, 11 carrier strike groups), and culturally (Hollywood, English lingua franca). The dollar accounts for ~59% of global reserves. This unipolar moment defined the 1990s and early 2000s.

China's GDP grew from $360bn (1990) to over $17 trillion by 2022, overtaking the US in PPP terms. The Belt and Road Initiative projects influence across 140+ countries. BRICS expanded in 2024 to include Iran, UAE, Egypt, Ethiopia. Multipolarity challenges American unipolarity, echoing Mackinder's Heartland Theory as Eurasian integration accelerates.

Joseph Nye distinguished hard power (military, sanctions) from soft power (cultural attraction, Confucius Institutes, K-pop, BBC World Service). Smart power combines both. The USA scores highly on soft power (universities, tech, media), while China invests heavily in soft assets to legitimise its rise without triggering a security dilemma.
